title: Safeguarded pool rebalance rollout: autoscaler handshake and eviction budgeting
creator: Asha Patel
summary: Implement a capacity-safe rollout mechanism for Dedicated GPU pools that coordinates drain waves with the cluster autoscaler and LTS channel gating to avoid request surges and SLA violations.
description: Background: Upgrading model-serving runtime on Dedicated GPU pools has historically caused transient capacity shortfalls when naive drains trigger autoscaler churn or tenant request surges. This ticket builds a controlled handshake protocol between the upgrade controller and the autoscaler, introduces a per-wave eviction budget calculator, and adds rollout gates tied to LTS channel compatibility and runtime-preserved session cache sizes. Goals: minimize request failures during upgrade, keep 99.9% throughput available for reserved tenants, and provide deterministic upgrade windows that operators can reason about. This will be used for LTS and non-LTS rollouts but must be conservative for LTS channels.
acceptance_criteria: Upgrade controller implements autoscaler_handshake_v2: plan -> reserve -> drain -> release sequence
Eviction budget computed per-pool and per-wave such that expected capacity loss <= configured pool_fallback_threshold (default 8%)
End-to-end e2e staging run with synthetic tenant traffic shows <0.5% error increase and median latency degradation <10% during waves
Canary run on 2 production pools without customer-facing errors and metrics monitored for 48 hours
Operator observable dashboard shows wave state, reserved capacity, autoscaler decisions, and predicted fallback before each wave
Runbook with rollback steps validated and a test DRILL executed in staging
runbook_steps: 1) Validate target pool has LTS channel affinity: check release.meta.lts_channel == true
2) Compute eviction_budget = floor(pool.available_gpus * pool.safety_fraction) with safety_fraction default 0.08; record as wave_max_evictions
3) Call autoscaler.reserve_capacity(pool_id, wave_max_evictions) and wait for ACK (timeout 3m)
4) If ACK, mark wave state=RESERVED and begin soft-drain: signal running instances with grace=45s to stop accepting new requests
5) Monitor queue depth and active_sessions; if active_sessions > expected_target after 60s, abort wave and call autoscaler.release_capacity
6) When active_sessions <= threshold, perform hard-evictions up to wave_max_evictions while keeping node_utilization >= min_utilization
7) Complete upgrade steps on drained nodes, run health checks, and reintroduce nodes to pool
8) Verify autoscaler ramps down reserved capacity via autoscaler.release_capacity and observe no negative SLO impact for 30m before next wave
9) If any step fails, follow rollback: stop upgrade, re-add nodes, trigger immediate rebalancing and notify on-call
design_decisions: Use an explicit reserve/release handshake with the autoscaler rather than relying on observation-only heuristics to reduce oscillation
Prefer soft-drain with a short grace window to give long-running KV cache-enabled sessions a chance to finish and avoid cache invalidation spikes
Eviction budget is conservative by default (8%) and configurable per-tenant for reserved pools to preserve contractual SLAs
Integrate rollout gates: block waves if runtime version mismatch, cache_max_bytes growth or model pinning would require incompatible quantization kernels
Expose telemetry for predicted vs actual capacity delta to enable offline tuning and ML-driven pacing later
tradeoffs: Conservative budgets increase total upgrade time (longer rolling windows) but reduce customer impact risk
Handshake protocol requires autoscaler API changes and adds code paths to both controller and autoscaler, increasing short-term engineering cost
Soft-drain increases tail latency for a brief period but avoids mass hard-evictions that cause higher error rates
Per-tenant configuration increases complexity of upgrade planner but is necessary for enterprise reserved pools
progress_updates: 2026-02-26: Spike completed — simulated wave execution in local simulator. Observed oscillation when reserve step was omitted.
2026-03-02: Prototype of autoscaler.reserve_capacity API submitted; initial mock accepted by infra team. See PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/autoscaler/pull/412
2026-03-05: Eviction budget calculator landed as library (pkg/upgrades/eviction_budget). Benchmarks show sensible outputs across skewed pool sizes.

2026-03-09: Staging run with 3 pools executed. Metrics: 0.3% error increase, median latency +6%, no SLA breach for reserved tenants. Observability dashboard prototype: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/upgrade-waves
2026-03-11: Security review kickoff — asked S&C for review on handshake auth model. Action: add signed reservation token to API calls (task assigned)
open_issues: Autoscaler API auth: need to decide between mTLS or signed tokens for controller->autoscaler reserve calls
Edge case: pools with very small size (<=3 GPUs) produce budget 0 if floor() applied; need fallback policy to allow single-node upgrades
Model-compatibility gating: define schema to express kernel/quantization incompatibilities in release metadata
Observability retention: wave-level traces need 7d retention for post-mortems but storage cost impact unclear
blockers: Autoscaler team needs to merge reserve/release endpoints (target milestone autoscaler-2.17)
S&C must sign off on reservation auth pattern before production rollout
